title: Family, articles and possessives
objectives: I can name my family members and say who is who in a photo.
I can explain why family words such as família, avô, irmã, tia and filho are spelled and pronounced as they are.
I can use definite and indefinite articles with the correct gender and number.
I can form regular plurals, including nouns that end in -ão, -l and -m, and explain why each ending behaves as it does.
I can say that something belongs to me, to you or to someone else, and choose between meu, minha, dele and dela for a reason.
I can talk about my pets, say what they are called and say whether I am single or married.

vocabulary.note: Stress and accent: fa-MÍ-li-a. The ending -ia counts as two syllables (i and a), so the stress falls on the third syllable from the end. No ending predicts that, so the acute accent is required. In speech the last two syllables often run together into one quick 'lyuh'.

The plural of o pai. The masculine plural is used for a group that includes at least one man, so os pais covers father and mother together. Do not confuse it with os países, the countries. Pai is one syllable with the diphthong ai, said like English 'eye'. País has a written accent on the í because the i is a syllable of its own (pa-ÍS), and the accent stays in países.
One syllable. The letters ai are a diphthong, two vowel sounds in one syllable, said like English 'eye', so no accent is needed.

The ending ãe is a nasal diphthong, said like English 'eye' through the nose. The tilde makes the vowel nasal. The word is a single syllable, so no stress mark is needed. Plural: as mães. Brazilians say mãe directly to their mothers, and mamãe is common for children.

ir-MÃO. Words ending in ão are stressed on the last syllable by default, so the tilde alone is enough: it marks the nasal sound. The plural is os irmãos, which means brothers, or brothers and sisters.
ir-MÃ. The ending ã is stressed on the last syllable by default, so the tilde only has to show the nasal vowel. It is the same word as irmão with the ending ã in place of ão.
The letters lh are one sound, like the 'lli' in English 'million': FEE-lyoo. Os filhos means sons, or, as the masculine plural, children in general.
The feminine of filho. The final a is a short, relaxed 'uh'.

a-VÔ. The ending o would put the stress on the second to last syllable, so stress on the last syllable needs an accent. The circumflex says the vowel is closed, like the o of English 'go' without the w glide. Avó, with an acute accent, is the grandmother. Often shortened to vô in speech.

a-VÓ. Same reasoning as avô, but the acute accent says the vowel is open, like the 'aw' of English 'law'. The only difference between avô and avó is this mark, so it carries the meaning. Often shortened to vó in speech.
The plural of avó, used as the masculine-plural word for grandfather and grandmother together. The accent stays: a-VÓS. Os avôs, with the circumflex, means grandfathers only.

In most of Brazil a t before the sound i is said like the 'ch' of 'cheese': TCHEE-oo. No accent is written because the stress is on the i by the default rule (ti-o ends in o, so the second to last syllable). The plural os tios means uncles, or uncles and aunts.
Said TCHEE-uh, by the same t-before-i rule. Brazilian children also call family friends and teachers tio and tia as a sign of affection.
English has one word for cousin. Portuguese marks the gender with the ending: o primo is a male cousin and a prima a female cousin. Os primos is male cousins or a mixed group.

example.target: O primo da Ana é alto.
example.source_literal: The cousin of-the Ana is tall.

vocabulary.note: ma-REE-doo. The d is a plain d because it comes before o: only d before the sound i is said like the 'j' of 'jeans'. The counterpart is a esposa.
A single s between two vowels is said z: es-PO-za. The everyday word is often a mulher, which means both the woman and the wife.
The letters nh are one sound, like the 'ny' of English 'canyon': so-BREE-nyoo. The feminine is a sobrinha. Os sobrinhos means nephews, or nephews and nieces.

example.source: My nephew is five years old.

vocabulary.note: The feminine is a neta. Os netos means grandchildren, by the masculine plural rule.

False friend, a word that looks like an English word but means something different: parente means a relative, any family member, and never 'parent'. The parents are os pais. Same form for men and women: o parente, a parente. Said pa-REN-tchee: the e before n is nasal, and t before the final e, which is said i, becomes 'ch'.

example.source: He is a relative of Ana.

vocabulary.note: Brazilian word. The letters ch are said like the 'sh' of 'shoe', and rr is the strong r, a breathy sound like English 'h': ka-SHO-hoo. The feminine is a cachorra. The word cão, plural cães, also means dog but is less common in everyday speech.
Feminine: a gata.

example.target: O gato da Ana é bonito.
example.source_literal: The cat of-the Ana is pretty.

vocabulary.note: Estimação comes from estimar, to hold dear. Said es-tchee-ma-SOWN: t before i is 'ch', the ç is said s before a, and the ending ão is stressed on the last syllable, so the tilde alone is enough. People also say pet.

example.target: Você tem um animal de estimação?
example.source_literal: You have an animal of esteem?

vocabulary.note: Means unmarried. Feminine: solteira. Said sow-tay-roo: the l at the end of a syllable sounds like w, and ei is the diphthong 'ay'. It agrees with the person: solteiro for a man, solteira for a woman.
Feminine: casada. The s between two vowels is said z: ka-ZA-doo. Related to casa, house; casar is to marry.
Feminine: a namorada. Namorado and namorada are used for a serious dating relationship, not only for casual dates.
The j is said like the s of English 'measure'. Same form for men and women. The plural is jovens: a final m is written n before the plural s. Used for people.
Feminine: nova. Said about an object it means new; said about a person it means young in age.

Se is a reflexive pronoun: it shows that the action goes back to the subject, here himself, herself or itself. Chama is the ele form of chamar, to call. Use it for people and pets. Eu me chamo is I am called. See the last grammar note.

grammar.title: Spelling and sound: the family words
grammar.explanation:
This lesson's words use almost every rule from the first three lessons, so this note reads them through, one rule at a time. Nothing here is new. The method is the one you already know: divide the word into syllables, find the stressed syllable, read the default from the ending, and write an accent only if the stress disagrees with the default. Then read each letter by the spelling rules. The table at the end lists the words with the rule behind each one.

Accents first. By default a word ending in a, e or o (with or without s), or in am, em or ens, is stressed on the second to last syllable, and a word ending in anything else is stressed on the last syllable. Família is fa-MÍ-li-a. The ending ia counts as two syllables, i and a, so the stress falls on the third syllable from the end, and no ending predicts that, so an accent is required (história and água work the same way). Avô and avó are a-VÔ and a-VÓ. The ending o predicts stress on the second to last syllable, the real stress is on the last, so an accent is required, and the quality of the vowel chooses the mark: the circumflex for the closed ô of avô, the acute for the open ó of avó. The two words differ only in that mark, and so does their meaning, grandfather against grandmother. Países is pa-Í-ses: the accent on the í shows that the i is a syllable of its own, so the word has three syllables, while pais, the parents, has one, with the diphthong ai. Têm gets its circumflex only to tell the plural they have from tem, he has; in Brazilian speech the two sound alike.

The tilde. Words in ã and ão need no further accent, because those endings are stressed on the last syllable by default: ir-MÃ, ir-MÃO. The tilde shows that the vowel is nasal, said with air through the nose, as in English 'sing' but without a trace of an n or ng sound afterwards. Mãe holds the nasal diphthong ãe, said like English 'eye' through the nose, and the ending ão is said like the 'ow' of 'now' through the nose. The tilde stays in the plural: irmãos, mães.

Now the consonants. Three digraphs, pairs of letters that spell one sound, appear: lh is said like the 'lli' of 'million' (filho), nh like the 'ny' of 'canyon' (sobrinho, minha), and ch like the 'sh' of 'shoe' (chama, cachorro). The rr of cachorro is the strong r, a breathy sound like English 'h'. A single s between two vowels is said z, which is why casado is ka-ZA-do and esposa is es-PO-za. The letters t and d change before the sound i: t is said like 'ch' of 'cheese' and d like the 'j' of 'jeans'. The sound i includes a final unstressed e, which is said i, so tio is TCHEE-oo, tia is TCHEE-uh, parente ends in -tchee and argentino is ar-zhen-TCHEE-noo. Before any other vowel the t and d are plain, so marido has an ordinary d. In argentino the g stands before e, so it is the soft sound of the 's' in 'measure', and the j of jovem is the same sound. In Recife the c stands before e, so it is said s.

Other words in the lesson's dialogues follow rules from the lesson on stress. A word stressed on the third syllable from the end always carries an accent, whatever its ending: médico is MÉ-di-ko and simpática is sim-PÁ-ti-ka. Francês and três are stressed on the last syllable, which breaks the default of an ending in s, so they need an accent, and the circumflex shows a closed vowel. The accent disappears in francesa and meses, because the stress is then on the second to last syllable, which the endings a and es already predict. The cedilla ç, as in engraçado and estimação, is a c said s before a, o or u. A letter h at the start of a word is silent, so Helena is eh-LEH-na. An r at the start of a word is the strong r, as in Recife and Rosa. The t of Tiago and Curitiba is said ch because an i follows it.

Nasal consonant letters. An m or n that ends a syllable is not a consonant sound; it only nasalizes the vowel before it. So the e of parente is nasal, jovem ends in a nasal 'ayn' without closing the lips, and quem is said 'kayn' (qu before e is k, and the u is silent). The same ending m turns into n when a plural s follows, a point the plural note uses.

Weak vowels and final l. A final unstressed a is said 'uh', a final unstressed o is said 'oo' and a final unstressed e is said 'ee', so filha ends in 'uh' and filho in 'oo'. The l at the end of a syllable is said like the w of 'now', so solteiro is sow-TAY-roo and animal ends in 'ow'. Finally, where no accent is written, the quality of a stressed e or o is not shown: nosso, 'our', has an open o, and cachorro a closed one. Learn it with the word.

a-VÔ: last-syllable stress breaks the default of o; closed vowel gives the circumflex
ah-VOH, closed o, no w glide
a-VÓ: same break; open vowel gives the acute
ir-MÃO: ão is stressed last by default, so the tilde only marks nasality
one syllable: the nasal diphthong ãe
pais has the diphthong ai (one syllable); países has the í alone (three syllables)
ch is sh; rr is the strong r
t before the sound i is said ch
d before o is a plain d
a single s between vowels is z
nasal e from the n; t before the final e, said i, is ch
l at the end of a syllable is w; ei is the diphthong ay
g before e is soft; n nasalizes; t before i is ch
stress on the third syllable from the end always needs an accent
last-syllable stress breaks the default of an ending in s; the circumflex shows a closed vowel
ç is a c said s before a, o or u
h at the start of a word is silent

grammar.title: Articles and noun gender
grammar.explanation:
An article is a small word placed before a noun to say whether you mean one particular thing that both speakers know (the definite article, 'the') or any one of its kind (the indefinite article, 'a' or 'an'). English has one of each, the and a or an, and they never change. Portuguese articles change, because they have a second job: they copy the gender and number of the noun. This is the agreement system from the grammar map. A noun fixes its gender, masculine or feminine, and its number, singular or plural, and the article must show the same. That is why each article has four forms, and why the article is the quickest label for a noun's gender: o means masculine singular, a feminine singular, os masculine plural and as feminine plural.

The indefinite article is um for a masculine noun and uma for a feminine noun. Um is also the number one, so um irmão is 'a brother' or 'one brother'. The plural uns and umas means 'some' or 'a few'. English has no plural of a, so it says 'some' or says nothing; Portuguese uses uns and umas less often than English uses 'some', and where English would just say 'cousins', Portuguese usually says primos with no article.

Gender is a property of the word, not of the thing. Most nouns ending in -o are masculine and most ending in -a are feminine, so the ending usually predicts the article: o filho, a filha; o tio, a tia. The exceptions have reasons. Several masculine nouns end in -a: o dia, o mapa, and the words in -ma that come from Greek, such as o problema and o sistema. A few feminine nouns end in -o: a mão keeps the gender of its Latin ancestor, and a foto and a moto are short for a fotografia and a motocicleta, so they keep the gender of the long word. The endings -ção, -são, -dade and -gem are normally feminine: a canção, a cidade, a viagem, and the -ção of estimação is the same ending. Nouns ending in -e have no reliable rule (o leite, a noite, o parente), so learn them with their article.

For people, the gender follows the person, and the family words show the ways Portuguese makes a pair. Most pairs swap the ending: filho and filha, tio and tia, primo and prima, neto and neta, sobrinho and sobrinha, namorado and namorada. Irmão and irmã swap ão for ã, and avô and avó differ only in the accent mark. Some pairs are two different words, as in English: o pai and a mãe, o marido and a esposa. A few nouns have one form for both sexes, and only the article changes: o parente, a parente.

A group takes the masculine plural when it contains at least one male or when the sex does not matter. Os filhos is sons, or sons and daughters together, so children; os tios is uncles, or uncles and aunts; os pais is the parents; os avós the grandparents. English has no such rule, which is why a Portuguese word list can look as if it gave only the masculine meaning. Only a group made entirely of women takes the feminine plural: as tias, as filhas.

Two uses of the definite article differ from English. First, in everyday Brazilian speech a first name usually takes the article, because the name is treated as a noun: a Ana, o Pedro. This is natural and not rude. The article is dropped when you speak straight to the person, as in Rosa's question Pedro, quem é ela?, against Pedro's reply Esta é a Juliana. Second, Portuguese keeps the article in general statements where English drops it: Os gatos são bonitos means 'Cats are pretty', and A família é importante means 'Family is important'. The Portuguese says, literally, 'the cats' and 'the family'.

examples.target: O pai da Ana é médico.
examples.source_literal: The father of-the Ana is doctor.

examples.target: A mãe do Pedro é professora.
examples.source_literal: The mother of-the Pedro is teacher.

examples.source: I have a brother and a sister.

examples.source_literal: The my grandparents are of Recife.

grammar.title: Regular plurals
grammar.explanation:
Number is whether you mean one thing, the singular, or more than one, the plural. English makes the plural almost always by adding -s or -es. Portuguese also adds an ending, but the ending depends on how the singular ends, and the logic is the same every time: the plural has to stay easy to say. A bare -s cannot be tacked on to every ending, so the last sound of the singular decides what happens. Learn that principle and you can predict most plurals.

After a vowel, add -s: casa, casas; filho, filhos; tio, tios. After -r or -z, add -es, because an r or z followed directly by s would be hard to say: mulher, mulheres; flor, flores; luz, luzes. The stressed syllable does not move, so no accent is needed: mulher is mu-LHER, mulheres is mu-LHE-res, and the default for the ending -es already stresses that syllable.

After -m, the m becomes n and the -s is added: homem, homens; jovem, jovens. This is the spelling rule from the lesson on sounds. An m or n at the end of a syllable only nasalizes the vowel, and the letter is m before p, b and at the end of a word, and n before any other consonant. The plural s is such a consonant, so the m turns into n, just as bom becomes bons.

After -l, the l is replaced by i and -s is added. This works because a final l is not really an l in Brazilian Portuguese: at the end of a syllable it is said like the w of 'now'. A w sound is a glide, the weak second part of a diphthong, and Portuguese writes the glide with the vowel letter i. So animal, said a-ni-MOW, becomes animais, with the diphthong ai. The same happens after e, o and u: papel becomes papéis, and azul becomes azuis. In papéis the stressed ending is the open diphthong éi, which Portuguese marks with an acute accent, while ai in animais needs no mark. Words ending in -il follow other patterns, which you will meet later.

Words ending in -s follow the stress. If the last syllable is stressed, add -es and watch the accent: país, países keeps its í because the i is still alone in its syllable, while mês becomes meses and loses its accent, because the new form now follows the default. If the last syllable is not stressed, the word does not change at all: o ônibus, os ônibus; o lápis, os lápis. Only the article shows the number.

Nouns in -ão have three possible plurals: -ões, -ães and -ãos. The three come from three different endings in Latin which merged into -ão in the singular and stayed distinct in the plural. Nothing in the singular spelling tells you which one a word takes, so learn the plural with each word. The ending -ões is by far the most common: limão, limões; avião, aviões; canção, canções. A few words take -ães: pão, pães; cão, cães. A few take -ãos, and the one you need now is irmão, irmãos; also mão, mãos. In every case the tilde stays, because the vowel is still nasal, and the stress stays on the last syllable.

The article and adjective become plural with the noun: os filhos altos, as tias simpáticas. The plural of avô is avôs, grandfathers, but os avós, the plural of avó, is the usual word for grandparents, by the masculine plural rule of the previous note. The accent of avôs and avós stays for the same reason as in the singular: the stress is on the last syllable, which breaks the default of the ending -os.

rows: after -r or -z add -es, so the s is pronounceable
-m is written n before a consonant
final l is a w glide, written i
same, and the open diphthong éi takes an acute
add -es; the í stays because it is alone in its syllable
unstressed last syllable in -s does not change

examples.target: Os pais dela são de Curitiba.
examples.source_literal: The fathers of-her are of Curitiba.

grammar.title: Possessives
grammar.explanation:
A possessive is a word that shows who something belongs to, or who is connected with it: my, your, our. English possessives agree with the owner: 'his father' and 'her father' differ because the owner is a man or a woman, and the thing owned changes nothing. Portuguese does the opposite. A possessive is treated like an adjective, so it agrees in gender and number with the thing owned, not with the owner. Minha irmã uses minha because irmã is feminine, whether the speaker is a man or a woman: a man says minha mãe and a woman says meu pai. To choose the form, look at the noun that follows and ignore who is speaking.

The four forms for 'my' are meu, minha, meus and minhas. For 'your', speaking to one person with você, they are seu, sua, seus and suas. For 'our' they are nosso, nossa, nossos and nossas, with an open o in the stressed syllable and an ordinary s sound for the ss. The digraph nh in minha is said 'ny': MEE-nya. The forms teu, tua, teus and tuas go with tu, which is regional, so you can skip them for now.

In Brazil the definite article before a possessive is optional: meu pai and o meu pai are both normal, and so are minha casa and a minha casa. European Portuguese nearly always keeps the article. If you keep it, it agrees with the noun too: os meus avós.

Seu and sua look like 'your', but they began as the possessives of the third person, meaning his, her or their. Because você is grammatically third person, as the lesson on pronouns explained, seu also came to mean your. So seu irmão can mean your brother, his brother, her brother or their brother, and the context has to decide. Brazilians avoid the doubt by putting dele (his), dela (her), deles (their, masculine or mixed) or delas (their, all female) after the noun: o irmão dele, a casa deles. These are literally 'of him', 'of her' and 'of them', and the next note shows why. For a group you are addressing, de vocês, 'of you all', is used: a casa de vocês.

The two systems agree with different things. Meu, minha, seu and sua agree with the thing owned. Dele, dela, deles and delas agree with the owner and never change for the thing owned: a casa dele and o carro dele both use dele, because the owner is a man, and o carro dela and a casa dela both use dela, because the owner is a woman.

A possessive without a noun is the word for 'mine' or 'yours': O cachorro é meu means 'The dog is mine'. A gente, we, takes nosso and nossa as nós does: a nossa casa; Brazilians also say a casa da gente, literally 'the house of the people'. In the question Qual é o seu nome? and the answer Meu nome é Ana, the possessives agree with nome, a masculine noun.

examples.target: Ele é meu irmão e ela é minha irmã.
examples.source: He is my brother and she is my sister.

examples.target: A casa de vocês é grande.
examples.source_literal: The house of you-all is big.

grammar.title: Whose: de, contractions, dele and dela
grammar.explanation:
English shows that something belongs to someone with an apostrophe and s before the thing: Ana's car. Portuguese has no apostrophe. It puts the thing first, then de, 'of', then the owner: o carro de Ana, literally 'the car of Ana'. English has the same pattern in 'the end of the day', but for people it prefers 's. In Portuguese the thing owned always comes first and the owner last: o gato do Pedro is 'Pedro's cat'. Whenever an English possessive ends in 's, rebuild it as thing + de + owner.

De is a preposition, a small word that links a noun to the rest of the sentence. As the grammar map explained, a preposition fuses with a following article into one word: de + o = do, de + a = da, de + os = dos, de + as = das. First names take the article in everyday Brazilian speech, so you hear o carro da Ana. Without the article de stays separate: o carro de Ana is also correct and a little more formal. The same fusion works when the owner phrase contains a possessive: a casa dos meus pais is de + os meus pais, and o gato da minha tia is de + a minha tia. Only the article fuses; the possessive stays as it is.

The same fusion explains dele and dela. De + ele = dele, de + ela = dela, de + eles = deles and de + elas = delas. So o irmão dele is literally 'the brother of-him', the same thing + de + owner pattern with a pronoun as the owner. This is why dele and dela mean his and her, and why they follow the owner (ele, ela, eles, elas) and not the thing owned.

To ask whose, Portuguese says 'of who': De quem é o cachorro? The word quem does not change and stays separate after de. The answer repeats the pattern: É do meu irmão, 'It is of-the my brother'.

examples.target: O carro da Ana é novo.
examples.source_literal: The car of-the Ana is new.

examples.target: O cachorro é do meu irmão.
examples.source_literal: The dog is of-the my brother.

examples.target: A casa dos meus avós é linda.
examples.source_literal: The house of-the my grandparents is lovely.

grammar.title: Having, being married and being called
grammar.explanation:
To say that you have a relative or a pet, Portuguese uses ter, just as English uses 'to have': Eu tenho dois irmãos. Ter is irregular: tenho, tem, temos, têm. In writing, têm with a circumflex is the plural, they have, and tem is he, she, you or a gente has; in speech both sound the same. The numbers one and two agree with the noun: um irmão and uma irmã, dois irmãos and duas irmãs.

A yes-or-no question is answered by repeating its verb: Você tem irmãos? Tenho, sim. Eles têm filhos? Têm, sim. Ela é casada? É, sim. The verb already carries the whole answer, and Portuguese prefers this to a bare sim. For no, put não before the verb: Não, não tenho.

Marital status is said with ser and an adjective, because it classifies the person in the same way as nationality or profession: Eu sou solteiro, Ela é casada. The adjective agrees with the person, so a man is solteiro or casado and a woman is solteira or casada. Jovem has one form for both sexes, and its plural is jovens. Brazilians also say estou solteiro or estou casado when they want to stress a present phase of life, but ser is the neutral choice. To say you are in a relationship, say Tenho namorado or Tenho namorada.

To say what a person or a pet is called, Portuguese uses the verb chamar, 'to call', with the pronoun se. A pronoun is a word that stands in for a noun, and a reflexive pronoun shows that the action goes back to the subject, 'himself', 'herself', 'itself'. English says 'The dog is called Totó', using a passive. Portuguese says, literally, 'The dog calls-itself Totó': O cachorro se chama Totó. Chamar is an -ar verb, so the forms are regular, with the reflexive pronoun changing for the person: eu me chamo, você se chama, ele se chama, a gente se chama, nós nos chamamos, vocês se chamam, eles se chamam. In everyday Brazilian speech the pronoun goes before the verb. The question is Como se chama o cachorro?, literally 'How calls-itself the dog?', or Como ele se chama?. You can also ask with the noun: Qual é o nome dele?, literally 'Which is the name of-him?', answered by O nome dele é Totó, literally 'The name of-him is Totó'.

examples.target: Eu tenho dois irmãos e uma irmã.
examples.source: I have two brothers and a sister.

examples.target: Ela é casada e ele é solteiro.
examples.source: She is married and he is single.
Do you have brothers or sisters? Yes, I do.

examples.target: Eles se chamam Mel e Bolinha.
examples.source: They are called Mel and Bolinha.

examples.target: Eu sou solteiro, mas tenho namorada.
examples.source: I am single, but I have a girlfriend.
examples.source_literal: I am single, but I-have girlfriend.

culture.title: Family life in Brazil
culture.text:
Family is at the center of Brazilian social life. Sunday lunch with parents, grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins is a weekly tradition for many families, and birthdays, baptisms and weddings are big events. Extended family is often close by, and it is common for adult children to live with their parents until they marry.

The words tio and tia are used very widely. Children call their parents' friends and their teachers tio and tia as a sign of affection, and a friend of the family can become tio Carlos or tia Rosa. Grandparents are often called vovô and vovó by small children, and vô and vó by adults; the accents work exactly as in avô and avó. Godparents, padrinho and madrinha, are an important part of the family too, and a child's parents and godparents call each other compadre and comadre, literally 'co-father' and 'co-mother', words also used between very close friends. A respectful title for an older woman is dona before her first name, as in dona Rosa.

Pets are increasingly part of the family. Dogs and cats are called animais de estimação, and many Brazilians treat them as members of the household. When people ask Você tem filhos? the answer may well be Tenho dois filhos e um cachorro. Family words are also used as terms of endearment. Strangers may address an older woman as tia or dona, and a street vendor may call a customer meu amigo or minha querida.

exercises.prompt: A man says '___ mãe é professora', meaning 'My mother is a teacher.' Which possessive fits?
exercises.explanation: A possessive agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner. Mãe is feminine singular, so minha, even though the speaker is a man.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'família' need a written accent?
choices: Every word ending in a vowel needs an accent
The i is a nasal vowel
The stress is on the third syllable from the end, which no ending predicts
exercises.explanation: The ending ia counts as two syllables, so fa-MÍ-li-a is stressed on the third syllable from the end. The default rule covers only the last and second to last syllables.

exercises.prompt: How is the t pronounced in 'tia'?
exercises.explanation: In most of Brazil a t before the sound i is said like 'ch': TCHEE-uh.

exercises.prompt: 'Avô' and 'avó' differ only in the accent. What does the circumflex in 'avô' tell you?
choices: The stress is on the first syllable
The o is closed, like the o of 'go' without the w glide
exercises.explanation: The circumflex marks a stressed closed vowel and the acute an open one. Avô is the grandfather, avó the grandmother.

exercises.prompt: Why is 'irmã' written with a tilde but no other accent, although it is stressed on the last syllable?
choices: Feminine words never take an accent
Words ending in ã are stressed on the last syllable by default, so the tilde only has to mark the nasal vowel
The tilde is another kind of acute accent
Because the word has only one syllable
exercises.explanation: An accent is needed only when the stress breaks the default of the ending. For ã and ão the default is the last syllable.

exercises.prompt: The final l of 'animal' is said like w. How does that explain its plural?
choices: The w sound is written with the vowel letter i, giving animais
exercises.explanation: A w sound is the glide of a diphthong, and Portuguese spells it i in the plural: animal becomes animais.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase means 'the children', a group of boys and girls together?
exercises.explanation: A group that includes at least one male takes the masculine plural. As filhas would mean daughters only.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase can only mean 'his sister', never 'her sister'?
exercises.explanation: Dele means of him. A sua irmã is ambiguous because sua can mean your, his, her or their.

exercises.prompt: In 'O marido dela é argentino', why is it 'dela' and not 'dele'?
choices: Dela is the plural of dele
Dela agrees with the owner, and the owner of the husband is a woman
exercises.explanation: Dele and dela follow the owner (de + ele, de + ela), never the thing owned.

exercises.prompt: Why is the plural of 'irmão' written 'irmãos' and not 'irmões'?
choices: Nouns in -ão have three plurals, -ões, -ães and -ãos, and each word must be learned
-ões is used only for feminine nouns
The tilde moves to the first syllable
exercises.explanation: The three plural endings come from three Latin endings that merged in the singular. -ões is the most common, but irmão, mão and a few others take -ãos.

exercises.prompt: In 'O cachorro se chama Totó', what does 'se' do?
choices: It is a reflexive pronoun: the action goes back to the dog, literally 'calls itself'
exercises.explanation: Se is the reflexive pronoun for ele, ela, você and a gente. Portuguese says the dog calls itself Totó where English says it is called Totó.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'simpática' need a written accent?
choices: It is stressed on the third syllable from the end, which no ending predicts
exercises.explanation: Sim-PÁ-ti-ka is stressed on the third syllable from the end. The default rule covers only the last and second to last syllables, so the accent is required, as in médico.

exercises.prompt: Why does 'francês' have an accent while 'francesa' does not?
choices: The accent marks a nasal vowel
Masculine words always take an accent
In francês the stress is on the last syllable, which breaks the default of an ending in s; in francesa the stress is on the second to last syllable, which the ending a predicts
exercises.explanation: An accent is written only when the stress breaks the default of the ending. Fran-CÊS breaks it; fran-CE-sa does not.
Avó is feminine singular, so the possessive is minha.
The number two agrees with the noun: dois irmãos, but duas irmãs.

exercises.prompt_target: ___ pais da Ana são de Recife.
exercises.explanation: Pais is masculine plural, so the article is os.
With the article before the name, de + a becomes da. Without the article, de stays separate.
The plural they have is written têm, with a circumflex. Tem, without it, is the singular.
Jovem ends in m, which is written n before the plural s: jovens. Novos, the plural of novo, also means young said of people.

exercises.prompt_target: Ele é meu irmão. A esposa ___ é brasileira.
exercises.hint_source: He is my brother. His wife is Brazilian.
exercises.explanation: Dele means of him. It follows the owner, who is male, and comes after the noun.

exercises.prompt_target: Ela é minha prima. O marido ___ é francês.
exercises.hint_source: She is my cousin. Her husband is French.
exercises.explanation: Dela follows the owner, who is female, even though marido is masculine.

exercises.hint_source: Their house is lovely (the women's house).
exercises.explanation: Delas is de + elas: of them, all female.
The final l is said like w, and the plural writes that glide as i: animal becomes animais.

exercises.prompt_target: Eu tenho dois ___ e uma irmã.
exercises.hint_source: I have two brothers and a sister.
exercises.explanation: Nouns in ão have three possible plurals. Irmão takes -ãos, not -ões.
Irmã is feminine, so minha. The article before a possessive is optional.
The plural they have is têm, with a circumflex.
Use thing + dele. Sua esposa could also mean your wife or her wife, so dele is clearer.

answers: O nome do cachorro é Totó.
exercises.explanation: Portuguese says the dog calls itself Totó, or uses the name of the dog.
